KEY MESSAGE 1...

In the mid/upper-levels, a subtropical ridge, objectively analyzed 
at 600 dam at 500 mb, was centered over the spine of the southern 
Appalachian Mountains. Phased, semi-progressive flow was displaced 
to the north of the CWA, or over the Great Lakes region, leaving the 
CWA beneath the northeastern fringe of the subtropical ridge as it 
begins to slowly retrograde westward. Isolated-to-widely-scattered 
showers and thunderstorms were ongoing as of 1619Z, with the bulk of 
these cells struggling to maintain intensity due to encountering 
larger-scale subsidence evident on water-vapor imagery. As the 
subtropical high gradually retrogrades throughout the afternoon and 
evening, it will cause the deep-layer flow to become more-westerly 
over the I-70 corridor, allowing ongoing clusters of showers or 
storms to potentially propagate southeastward along the thickness 
gradient and into the northwestern portions of the CWA.

At the surface, a synoptic cold front was drawn along a line from 
TOL-IND, and is expected to remain quasi-stationary, with a slow 
progression towards the south, over the next 24 hours due to the 
northern displacement of more-amplified flow aloft. Thus, the 
boundary-layer will remain relatively homogeneous this afternoon, 
with temperatures set to peak in the lower 90s. NBM initialized 
dewpoints that were far too high, and were adjusted downward a few 
degrees (CONSAll) to match observations from yesterday. Such an 
adjustment yields heat indices in the upper 90s across southeastern 
OH, although some locales may reach 100 degrees. Surface winds were 
calm, and will remain calm, throughout the rest of today and into 
tonight while transitioning to the east after sunset due to the 
gradual departure of the surface and mid-level anticyclones.

The Special Weather Statement previously issued for the hot and 
humid conditions today has been extended through 23Z, or 7 PM EDT, 
for the lowlands. Anvil shadows from storms that develop upstream of 
the OH River this afternoon may offset hotter temperatures from 
coming to fruition, but the expectation is for storm coverage to 
remain isolated-to-widely-scattered at best this afternoon and 
evening. The 12Z RAOBs from WFOs ILN and RNK sampled a well-defined 
warm nose in the mid-levels, which will suppress more-widespread 
development despite convective temperatures being reached. Storms 
that can develop and mature will be capable of producing locally 
heavy rainfall, in addition to strong-to-marginally-severe-caliber 
downbursts, due to sufficient water-loading of updrafts atop the 
well-mixed boundary-layer (i.e., Inverted-V PBL profiles, with a PBL 
top near 3.5 kft AGL). The best potential for storms this afternoon 
and evening will be along and northwest of the Ohio River. Prospects 
for showers and storms will wane following the cessation of vertical 
mixing, with valley fog expected to develop across portions of the 
lowlands and into the mountainous terrain tonight.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

By sunrise Thursday morning, the center of the subtropical ridge 
will have retrograded to the middle MS River Valley while an 
intense, shortwave trough digs southeastward over the southern edge 
of the Hudson Bay. The superposition of these features relative to 
the CWA will allow a train of shortwave perturbations emanating from 
the core of the phased jetlets over the Great Lakes to propagate 
southeastward into the CWA. Isolated-to-widely-scattered, elevated 
showers and storms may be ongoing across the northern counties prior 
to sunrise as the leading shortwave perturbation ejects over the 
region. The pre-frontal airmass across the CWA will be characterized 
by anomalously high PWATs around 2.00" amidst tall, skinny CAPE 
profiles, with SBCAPE values between 2,000-2,500 J/kg and very warm 
surface temperatures. (The 12Z RAOB from WFO ILN this past morning 
also sampled SBCAPE of 2,356 J/kg.) Widespread cloud cover may limit 
the degree of destabilization Thursday afternoon; however, with the 
arrival of the aforementioned synoptic cold front in Key Message 1, 
the frontogenetical forcing and ejection of a well-defined shortwave 
perturbation will yield scattered-to-numerous showers and storms 
Thursday afternoon and evening. 

Effective-shear magnitudes of about 25 kt will contribute to small, 
compact hodographs, with mean shear vectors orthogonally-oriented to 
the slow-moving cold front. Upshear Corfidi vectors of less than 10 
kt favor the potential for back-building cells, especially along the 
front since it will be slow to progress. A few swaths of heavy 
rainfall are forecast to affect portions of the CWA Thursday, as 
downshear Corfidi vectors remain at about 25 kt while nearly aligned 
to the mean wind. It remains unclear on where exactly back-building 
cells will originate, but an eventual southward propagation to the
